doc.title: perf(daemon): github-counters summary parses the whole request log every time
doc.body:
## Problem

`GithubCountersService` (`src/daemon/services/github_counters.rs`, #1387) builds every summary by reading the **entire** request log: `github_metrics::aggregate` opens `log.jsonl` and JSON-parses every line into a `LogRecord` *before* it checks the record kind or the `since` window. The cost is O(total log size), and the log is unbounded by default (rotation and prune are opt-in, `OMNI_DEV_LOG_MAX_SIZE`).

The module doc says the opposite: "Every emission is best-effort and bounded (a small local log read, no network), so it never delays shutdown." That holds only while the log is small.

The scan runs:

- ~5s after daemon startup,
- every 10 minutes,
- once in `shutdown()`, which `registry.shutdown_all()` awaits before the process can exit,
- on every `daemon status` (`status()` calls it), and on every `summary` op.

By reading the code, the last two mean `daemon status` also waits on a full scan. I have not timed that one.

## Evidence

- #1653 sampled a daemon mid-shutdown on a 4.1 GB log: ~200% CPU with every hot stack in `aggregate` → `serde_json::from_str::<LogRecord>`. Startup summary landed 75 s after "listening" (debug build) and the shutdown summary 53 s after "shutting down".
- Reproduced on 2026-10-03 with a 4.7 GB log: a throwaway `daemon run --services worktrees` sat at ~100% CPU from ~5 s after start, and did not exit on SIGTERM or SIGINT until killed with SIGKILL after about a minute.
- Control: the same daemon with `OMNI_DEV_LOG_FILE` pointing at an empty file idled at 0% CPU and stopped gracefully on SIGTERM. The log read is the only variable.
- The service is registered unconditionally (`daemon.rs`), so `--services` does not turn it off; the repro above had `--services worktrees`.

#1653 / #2044 fixed this for the **tests** (they now point `OMNI_DEV_LOG_FILE` at a tempdir). The production daemon still pays it on every startup, restart or upgrade, and every 10 minutes. #1653 listed this as a recommended follow-up, and I could find no issue for it.

## Proposal

Make each summary cost O(records appended since the last one), not O(log).

The daemon only ever wants "records since I started", and the log is append-only. So the service can remember `(file identity, byte offset, running tally)`:

- At construction, record the log's current length and identity (inode, or the platform equivalent). The boot baseline is then a zero tally.
- On each summary (`emit`, `status`, `summary`), read only the bytes after the stored offset, add those records to the running tally, and advance the offset.
- If the file's identity changed or its length is below the stored offset (rotation, or `omni-dev log prune`'s atomic rewrite), fall back to a windowed full scan and reset the offset. A shrinking or replaced file must never produce a silently wrong tally.
- Keep reading complete lines only: a partial trailing line from a concurrent writer is left for the next read.

An alternative is to read the file backwards and stop at the first record older than `started_at`. That is simpler to reason about but is not robust to concurrent writers whose timestamps interleave slightly, so I'd lean towards the offset approach.

`aggregate` itself stays as is for `omni-dev log count` and the `gh` CLI summaries, which legitimately want an arbitrary window.

Separately, the final flush in `shutdown()` is currently unbounded. Even after the above it is worth asking whether shutdown should ever wait on a file read, since `spawn_blocking` work cannot be cancelled.

## Acceptance

- The cost of `emit`, `status` and `summary` does not grow with the size of `log.jsonl` before daemon start. A test can assert it: a fixture with many pre-boot records must not have those records parsed.
- The counts match what the full scan produces for the same window, including records appended by other processes after boot and a partial trailing line.
- Rotation and prune (file replaced, or shorter than the stored offset) fall back to a correct full scan.
- A daemon started against a multi-GB log reaches its startup summary and exits on SIGTERM in about the time it takes with an empty log.
- The module doc's "bounded, never delays shutdown" claim is true, or is corrected.

## Related

#1387 (the counters), #1653 and #2044 (the test-side fix and the root-cause analysis). Unbounded default growth of `log.jsonl` is a separate decision; #1121 added the opt-in bounds.

comments.author: newhoggy
comments.body:
## Implementation plan

Settled after reading `github_counters.rs`, `github_metrics::aggregate`, and the `request_log` writer, rotation and `prune` code. It takes the byte-offset approach the issue leans towards, and also closes the two other places the daemon can wait on a scan at shutdown.

### What else waits on a scan today

Besides the `shutdown()` flush, two more paths can block on one:

- `shutdown()` first awaits the logger task. The logger's `emit` runs inside a `select!` arm, so cancelling the token is not seen until the in-flight scan finishes. A SIGTERM that arrives during the 5 s startup scan therefore waits for that whole scan, then for the shutdown scan.
- `main` drops the tokio runtime on exit, and that waits for outstanding `spawn_blocking` work. A scan whose `await` was abandoned would still hold the process open, so a timeout around the `await` alone would not help. The scan itself has to notice it should stop.

### Design

**1. Engine: `github_metrics::IncrementalCounts`** (new `src/github_metrics/incremental.rs`, re-exported from `github_metrics`). It holds `path`, `since`, a running `GhCounts`, and a cursor of `{ file id, offset, tail }`.

- The cursor `offset` is always just past a `\n`, so only complete lines are ever consumed and a partial trailing line is left for the next read.
- **Baseline (`start`)**: stat the log *before* reading the clock. A record stamped at or after `since` was then necessarily appended after the baseline, so the bytes we read next contain every such record. The baseline offset is aligned back to the last complete line, since a concurrent writer may be mid-line. Nothing is parsed. A missing log means no cursor, and the first refresh scans the new file from byte 0.
- **`refresh(stop)`**: open the path, identify that exact file, validate the cursor, then read lines from `offset` with `read_until(b'\n')`. Each line goes through the same window, source and kind check as `aggregate`, and the offset advances only past complete lines.
- **Cursor validation.** The cursor is kept only if all three hold:
  - the file id is unchanged (dev+ino on unix);
  - `len >= offset`;
  - the last 64 bytes before `offset`, kept in the cursor, are unchanged.

  Otherwise the file was replaced by `prune`, rotated, truncated, rewritten in place, or seen for the first time, and the tally is dropped and rebuilt by a windowed scan from byte 0. That is exactly the fallback the issue asks for, and it gives what `aggregate` gives. A missing file yields zero counts, as `aggregate` does. The byte check is what catches `: > log.jsonl` followed by regrowth past the old offset, and inode reuse; length and inode alone cannot. The engine deliberately does not hold the old file open to pin its inode: after a `prune` that would keep the multi-GB pre-prune file allocated on disk until the next refresh.
- **Cooperative stop.** `refresh` takes `stop: impl FnMut() -> bool`, checked before each line. On stop it returns `complete = false` with the state consistent at a line boundary, and the next refresh resumes there, so no work is lost. A read error does the same and is logged at debug.
- **Shared filter.** The per-record check moves out of `aggregate` into one private function that both scans call, so the full scan and the incremental one agree by construction. `aggregate`'s signature and behaviour are unchanged; `omni-dev log count` and `omni-dev github count` still use it.

**2. Service: `GithubCountersService`**

- It holds `Option<Arc<Mutex<IncrementalCounts>>>` (`None` when no log path resolves) and a service-wide `stopping` `CancellationToken`. `new()` becomes `with_log_path(request_log::log_file_path())`, so tests inject a temp path (STYLE-0028) instead of reading the developer's real log.
- `emit`, `status` and the `summary` op refresh that tally on a blocking thread instead of calling `aggregate`. The `std::Mutex` is taken only on the blocking thread, never across an `.await`, and poison is recovered with `into_inner`.
- **Shutdown** cancels `stopping` first, which ends the logger loop and aborts any in-flight periodic, `status` or `summary` scan. It then awaits the logger and emits the final summary under a 2 s deadline. If the deadline hits, the line is logged marked incomplete rather than delaying exit. The logger's own per-task token is replaced by `stopping`.
- A refresh that did not finish is surfaced: the summary line says `(incomplete)` and the `summary` op adds `"incomplete": true`, only when true, so existing consumers see no change.

**3. Docs.** Correct the "bounded, never delays shutdown" claim in the module doc and the matching comment in `daemon.rs`, update the daemon paragraph in `docs/log.md`, and add a `### Fixed` entry to `CHANGELOG.md`.

### Tests

Engine, with `tempfile` fixtures and no timing assertions:

- Pre-boot records are never read. They are valid `gh` records with future timestamps, so a full scan would count them and the tally must not. The cursor offset must equal the baseline file length.
- Parity with `aggregate(path, Some(since), ..)` over a mix of `gh` and non-`gh` records, a record stamped before `since`, malformed and blank lines, and appends across several refreshes with no double counting.
- A partial trailing line: not counted until its newline arrives, then counted once. Also a baseline taken mid-line, and one where the partial line is longer than the backward-scan block.
- Fallback to a full scan, each compared to `aggregate`: file replaced (`prune`-style rename over), rotated, removed then recreated, truncated shorter than the offset, truncated and regrown past the offset with different content (the tail-bytes check), and a log absent at start then created.
- `stop`: halts at a line boundary with `complete = false`, and a later refresh catches up to equal `aggregate`.

Service:

- Starting against a fixture with many pre-boot records and then appending: `status` and `summary` count only the appended ones.
- Shutdown against that fixture emits and returns.
- The existing service test is switched to an injected temp path, so it no longer reads the real log.

### Verification

- `cargo test` for the touched modules, `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt`, `./scripts/build.sh`, and `cargo doc --no-deps --document-private-items` (CI denies broken intra-doc links).
- A/B against the acceptance criterion: a synthetic multi-GB `log.jsonl` pointed to by `OMNI_DEV_LOG_FILE`, `daemon run --services worktrees` on an isolated socket, measuring CPU after the startup summary and the time to exit on SIGTERM. The released v0.45.0 binary has the bug and serves as the baseline; this branch is compared against it.

### Decisions and non-goals

- **Rotation resets the tally.** The issue defines the full scan as the oracle, and `aggregate` reads only the live `log.jsonl`, so records rotated into `log.jsonl.1` stop being counted, exactly as today. Carrying the tally across a rotation (the old file is now `.1`) is possible, but `prune` cannot be told apart from a rotation by the live file alone, so it is left as a possible follow-up.
- `aggregate` gets no `kind` prefilter, and `log count` is untouched.
- No new trust boundary, no CLI surface change (so no `update-snapshots` run), no ADR needed.
- Unbounded default growth of `log.jsonl` stays a separate decision (#1121).

### Acceptance mapping

| Acceptance criterion | Covered by |
|---|---|
| Cost of `emit`, `status`, `summary` does not grow with pre-boot log size | Baseline-by-offset, plus the future-timestamp test |
| Counts match the full scan, including other processes' appends and a partial trailing line | The shared filter, plus the parity tests |
| Rotation and prune fall back to a correct full scan | Cursor validation, plus the fallback tests |
| A daemon on a multi-GB log reaches its startup summary and exits on SIGTERM as fast as with an empty log | The A/B run |
| "Bounded, never delays shutdown" is true or corrected | Cooperative stop and the 2 s shutdown deadline, plus the corrected docs |

### Commits

1. `perf(lib)`: the `IncrementalCounts` engine, the shared filter and the engine tests.
2. `fix(daemon,docs,changelog)`: wire the service onto it, with the shutdown handling, service tests, docs and changelog.

doc.title: Sessions: count events recovered from the hook journals so dropped POSTs are measurable
doc.body:
## Problem

#2108 added a durable journal behind the hook sink, so an event whose socket POST is dropped is recovered by the daemon. There is no way to see how often that happens. The issue asked to measure how often the 2s hook timeout drops events "from `log.jsonl`, before and after", and that turns out to be only partly possible.

Measured over 8 hours on 2026-10-03 from the invocation records (`duration_ms` of `sessions hook`):

| Binary | Hook runs | p99 | Max | Runs at or over 1s |
|--------|-----------|-----|-----|--------------------|
| 0.43.0 | 8,763 | 59 ms | 624 ms | 0 |
| 0.45.0 | 1,140 | 57 ms | 2,002 ms | 1 |

The one 2,002 ms run coincided with a daemon restart (SIGTERM at 13:52:36, connections draining until 13:52:41), and the journal held the event it lost. So the log shows that a timeout is essentially never hit while the daemon is healthy.

It cannot show the other kind of drop. A connection refused returns in a few milliseconds and the sink exits 0, so it looks the same as a delivered event. Any real count of drops has to come from the daemon.

## Proposal

Count how each event reached the registry, and show it in `daemon status` and the `sessions` status detail.

- `socket`: events applied from the socket.
- `recovered`: events applied from a journal whose socket copy never arrived. These are the dropped POSTs.
- `replayed`: events applied by a journal's first-sight replay (startup, or a new file).

`recovered` must not count a race. The journal watcher can read a line in the millisecond between a hook writing its journal and its POST arriving. The POST then arrives as a duplicate. At 5s polling that is about 0.02% of events, a few a day, which is the same size as the signal, so the counter has to subtract it. Remember which route each recent `seq` came by, and count a socket event that duplicates a journal-applied `seq` as `socket_after_journal`; `recovered` is journal-applied minus that.

Needs a third `Origin` for a first-sight replay, so replay is counted apart from tail catch-up while the dedupe and staleness rules stay shared.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `daemon status` shows the three counts for the sessions service, and `daemon status --json` carries them under the sessions detail.
- [ ] A POST that never arrives counts as `recovered`; one that arrives just after the journal poll does not.
- [ ] Counters are monotonic since the daemon started and are not persisted.
- [ ] Documented in `docs/sessions-service.md`, with how to read them (a steady `recovered` of 0 means the socket is keeping up).

Follow-up to #2108.

doc.title: yq: --ascii-output's json_ascii! wrap costs +0.49% on the default JSON path (x86_64) via code size
doc.body:
**Severity: Low** (a small, measured, deliberately accepted regression with a known fix)

## Summary

#1983 (fixing #1700) knowingly traded ~0.5% of the **default** `-o json` streaming path on
x86_64 for `--ascii-output`'s correctness. This issue tracks buying it back.

The `json_ascii!` macro in `yq_runner.rs` duplicates its body across both arms so the
default path keeps *exactly* the code it had before — no per-write branch, no extra layer
between the M2 streamers and the writer. The cost is therefore **code size, not a lost
inline**: each streamer is monomorphized twice across the six use sites.

| | arm64 | x86_64 |
|---|---|---|
| release binary | +108 KB (+1.3%) | +123 KB (+1.1%) |

## Measurement

Interleaved A/B of the *default*, non-`--ascii-output` path — `.` and `.[]` over 1 MB and
10 MB `users`/`navigation` documents, 7 reps, output identity gated, `scripts/ab-cli.py`:

| Machine | Median | Rows slower | Control floor (same corpus) |
|---|---|---|---|
| AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (x86_64) | **+0.49%** | **8 of 8** | −0.00% median, 4-of-8 slower |
| Apple M4 Pro (ARM64) | −1.21% | 0 of 8 | −0.48% median |

Small, but the sign consistency on x86 is what makes it real rather than noise — the rule
`ab-cli.py` prints itself. Worth noting for anyone re-measuring: **a broader corpus hides
this.** An earlier run over 5 patterns x 2 MB read +0.08% with a mixed 6/10 slower and was
(wrongly) called neutral. Concentrate the corpus on the shapes that actually stress the
streaming path, and always take the machine's own `--control` floor on the same corpus.

This is #965's effect arriving by a different route — size rather than a lost inline — so
"the default path's source is unchanged" did not imply "no regression".

## The fix

Stop instantiating the streamers a second time: give the `--ascii-output` arm a
`&mut dyn Write` and leave the default arm concrete. That pays a vtable call only on the
branch that is already doing per-character escaping (where it is noise against the escape
work itself), and returns the default arm to a single monomorphization.

Worth confirming afterwards that the binary-size delta is gone and that the x86 default-path
rows return to the control floor, on the same corpus as above.

## Related

- #1700 / #1983 — where the trade was made and documented (see `json_ascii!`'s doc comment).
- #965 — the original measurement of this call graph's inlining/code-size sensitivity.

comments.author: newhoggy
comments.body:
## Triage (2026-09-04) — fix is a measurement; the proposed `dyn` shape does not restore a single instantiation

Confirmed on 147fc1638: `json_ascii!` (`yq_runner.rs`) with six sites — both `stream_cursor!` JSON arms, the two `stream_json_document` `_ =>` fallbacks, `--slurp`'s `stream_json_sequence`, `--inplace`'s `FmtWriter`. Sink types: 5× `&mut ColorSink<'_, W>` (stdout writer), 1× `FmtWriter<BufWriter<File>>`.

**Correction to the issue's fix sketch.** Giving only the `--ascii-output` arm a `&mut dyn fmt::Write` still leaves every streamer instantiated twice: once for the concrete sink and once for `&mut dyn Write` (`impl Write for &mut W where W: ?Sized`). It collapses the *ascii* instantiations across the two distinct sink types (2 → 1), so the saving is at most about half the +123 KB, and whether the x86 +0.49% follows is exactly what the A/B has to say. The shape that does return each streamer to one instantiation per sink type is to fold ASCII escaping into `ColorSink` itself (a fourth variant, or a `bool` consulted in `ColorSink::write_str`, which is already a `match`) — cost one predictable branch per `write_str` span, not per character; the macro's doc rejected that on assumption, not measurement.

### Decision
Build **both** candidates — (A) the issue's `dyn` arm and (B) ASCII escaping folded into `ColorSink` — and A/B each against today's main under the protocol below. Ship whichever clears the control floor on x86 with the smaller binary; if neither does, keep the macro and record the measured numbers in the issue and `docs/parsing/yaml.md`.

**Protocol** (docs/guides/benchmarking.md § A/B, `scripts/ab-cli.py`): same build profile for base (`147fc1638`) and candidates; corpus `users`/`navigation` at 1 MB and 10 MB (rule 2: ≥ 1 MB); queries `.` and `.[]`; `-o json`, no `-a`; `--reps 7`; run `--control` first on each host and quote its floor; interleaved (rule 1 — the script does it); output identity gated (rule 4) including vs real yq; report all 8 rows + median per host, on both pinned machines — ARM `johns-mac-mini` (M4 Pro) and x86 `terminus` (Ryzen 9 7950X); also report release-binary size delta on both, plus one `-a` row per host to show the ascii path is not regressed beyond noise; box idle (`ps -Ao pcpu`), AC power. Acceptance: x86 default-path median inside the control floor and no longer 8-of-8 slower; binary size back within ~+20 KB of pre-#1983; `test_ascii_output_covers_every_live_json_route_1700` green.
Blocked on access to the two benchmark hosts; not Sonnet-shaped if the first candidate fails the gate (judgement call on what to try next).

doc.title: yq: -R rows for the --jq-extensions string builtins (ltrimstr, startswith, ascii_downcase) sit above the DOM route ceiling (#3479 follow-up)
doc.body:
## What

`succinctly yq --jq-extensions -R` over the jq-only string builtins `ltrimstr`, `startswith` and `ascii_downcase` is slower than the route it replaced, by more than the ceiling the DOM route is now judged against. #3479 closed on that ceiling (+10% wall-clock, about +5% instructions for a yq-native `-R` row, recorded in `docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md`); these rows are not yq-native, so the document names them as the exception above it instead of judging them against it. This issue is where that exception is tracked.

## What is on record

Measured as merged in #3535 (10 MB of `-R` lines of the `users` document, median wall-clock, interleaved `scripts/ab-cli.py`, 9 reps, output identity gated, against the pre-#3535 base `98e7631a4`):

| row                              | M4 Pro | 7950X |
|----------------------------------|--------|-------|
| `startswith("{")` (`--jq-extensions`) | +19%   | +13%  |
| `ltrimstr("{")` (`--jq-extensions`)   | +13%   | +16%  |

`limitations.md` gives the range over the three builtins as +9% to +19%. Controls read -5%..+3% (M4 Pro) and -4%..+3% (7950X), so these are outside the noise floor on both chips.

The documented cause is the one every bridged builtin shares: with no native arm in the generic evaluator, the call decodes the value, writes it out and indexes it again, once per `-R` line. #3642 and #3679 narrowed that for the rows they could (a partial slice, and a scalar line the owned fast path knows); #3679 says in its own body that it does not change these rows and does not re-measure them.

## Not yet established

- **Whether the figures still hold.** They predate #3642 and #3679 and have not been re-measured since. `ascii_downcase` has no row in the table above; the documented +9% to +19% range includes it, but its own figure is not on record.
- **Which call sites bridge.** The cause above is the documented one, not one profiled for these three builtins.

## Reaching it

Only under the flag; without it yq's own lexer rejects the builtins, so a default `succinctly yq -R` never gets here:

```console
$ printf '{"a":1}\n' | succinctly yq --jq-extensions -R 'ltrimstr("{")'
"a":1}
$ printf 'User7\n' | succinctly yq -R 'ascii_downcase'
Error: parse error at position 0: "ascii_downcase" is not part of yq's syntax; pass --jq-extensions to enable succinctly's jq-compatible builtin surface
```

## Plan

1. **Re-measure first**, on the M4 Pro and the 7950X, with the method in `docs/guides/benchmarking.md` (interleaved, 9 reps, 1 MB and 10 MB, a control, and the inert-padding holdout for any x86 row), against the pre-#3535 base and current `main`. Add `ascii_downcase`, which has no figure. Gate on output identity.
2. **If a row is still above the ceiling**, attribute it before choosing a fix (build once with the bridge disabled for that builtin, rather than trusting a profile alone), then give it a native arm in `eval_generic.rs` that mirrors `eval.rs`'s semantics. Both evaluators answer this builtin, so the fix needs the dual-evaluator checks (parity tests and the differential/fuzz sweeps with the DOM-forcing flags). A native arm also moves cursor-route cost, so run `scripts/perf-guard.py` and accept any movement deliberately.
3. **If every row is now under the ceiling**, close this with the numbers and update the exception in `limitations.md`.

## Priority

Low. Default yq is unaffected, the rows exist only behind an opt-in extension flag, and the cost is +9% to +19% on a per-line basis. It is worth doing only if the re-measurement still shows a gap.

Related: #3479 (closed on the ceiling), #3535, #3642, #3679.

Posted by Claude Code at the request of the maintainer.

- The first two are 270 s of 822 s (33%). The other ~4,480 tests sum to ~340 s.

It is intrinsic to the check; do not shrink the stack or change `opt-level` for the test profile to speed it up, since the native-stack-floor tests depend on frame sizes.
- On CI the long pole shows as `tests/jq_cli_tests.rs` taking ~319 s on x86_64 debug. `Test (macOS ARM64) (cli-gated)` (8.2 min) is the macOS critical path since #3655.

## Proposal

Add a `deep-recursion` leg to each of the x86_64, ARM64 and macOS ARM64 matrices running just those two tests by name (`cargo test --features cli --test jq_cli_tests -- --exact <name> <name>`), and add `-- --skip <name> --skip <name>` to the existing `jq_cli_tests` invocation in `cli-gated`. Rough estimate, not measured on CI: `cli-gated` test time falls from ~(822 / cores) to ~(552 / cores), and the new leg takes about as long as the slowest test (~150 s locally plus build).

## Cost / risks

- One extra job per platform, three in all. #3064's problem was macOS slot contention, so re-measure macOS queue wait after the change.
- The skip list and the new leg must stay in step, or a test silently stops running. Guard it: the leg's `--exact` names must match, and a renamed test fails loudly there, but a stale `--skip` in `cli-gated` would not. Consider a check that both lists name existing tests.
- Other long tests in the same family (the `*_2135`, `*_1371`, `*_3296` group, 20-26 s each) could join later; start with the two.
